title: Why are these friends alike?
hook: Every friendship here joins two people of the same colour. How did it get that way?

doesNotKnow: that 'people choose similar friends' and 'friends make each other similar' can leave the identical snapshot, so a snapshot cannot say which happened

misconception: If friends are alike, they must have chosen each other for it.
objective: The learner can explain that a picking history (links change, colours fixed) and a copying history (colours change, links fixed) can end in the identical picture, so one snapshot cannot separate selection from influence, and that telling them apart needs data over time.

claims.text: The two histories on the stage end in the same picture: the same 12 friendships (each group of 4 fully linked) and the same colours, so all 12 friendships join same colours.
claims.source: town1(3) and town2(2) in src/demos/probability/same-picture-two-histories/Demo.tsx both equal FINAL_LINKS (two 4-cliques, 6 + 6 = 12) with colours 0000 1111; the stage tests sameFrame() and shows '= final'. Brief check: node company/courses/ncm/checks/rejudged-four.mjs, J9 {"links":12,"identicalFinal":true}. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: Town 1 changes 3 friendships and no colours (it starts with 3 friendships joining different colours and swaps one per step for a same-colour friendship); Town 2 changes 2 colours and no friendships (person 3, then person 7, takes their friends' colour).

claims.text: So a single snapshot cannot separate choosing similar friends from becoming like your friends; telling them apart needs data over time: who changed first, the link or the person.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 4 (section 4.2 unconfirmed: selection and social influence both produce homophily, and separating them needs longitudinal data). Aral, Muchnik and Sundararajan (2009), 'Distinguishing influence-based contagion from homophily-driven diffusion in dynamic networks', PNAS 106(51): 21544-21549, for the identification problem. Shown on the stage by c1 and c2. Attribution: fact-checker confirms.

recall.question: A one-time survey of a school finds that runners' friends are mostly runners. What can that survey alone tell you?
options: Runners pick other runners as friends
Not which: picking friends and copying friends can both leave this pattern
recall.why: Choosing similar friends and becoming like your friends can end in the identical snapshot. Telling them apart needs data over time: whether the friendship or the running came first.
